newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD greets French vote, CDU thinks of Europe.
newsitem.headline: German SPD greets French vote, CDU thinks of Europe.

text.p: Germany's left-wing opposition chief Oskar Lafontaine hailed French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin's victory in the parliamentary election on Sunday as a "a great success for France and for Europe."

A leading German conservative politician, though, said the change of government would lead to intensified talks between Bonn and Paris about the future of Europe's planned monetary union (EMU) and social issues facing the 15-nation bloc.

German radio and television stations gave the vote top priority on Sunday evening and first commentaries said President Jacques Chirac had failed dramatically in his bid to remodel his government to prepare France for EMU.
Preliminary results late on Sunday evening gave the combined left an absolute majority of at least 289 seats in the 577-seat National Assembly.
"This is a great success for France and for Europe," said Lafontaine, who would like to copy next year the successes of Jospin and Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.
"With it are linked the people's hopes for a reduction in unemployment and for more social justice," the Social Democrat (SPD) chairman said in his message of congratulations.

Karl Lamers, foreign policy spokesman for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), focussed on the European implications of the left-wing victory in France, until now Germany's main ally in the drive to launch EMU in 1999.
"I would expect the debate that has already begun to take place over the direction of economic and social policies to intensify," Karl Lamers told Hesse Radio.
"I do not expect any change," Lamers said of Franco-German ties when asked if a socialist government would bring any major shift in foreign policy.
"I am pleased that the Socialists at least will be strong enough to have the decisive voice in government," he said, echoing comments made about Blair's large majority.

Lamers said talks about the future of the single European currency, along with efforts by Germany and France to meet entry criteria for its start in 1999, would be a top issue as both nations sought to cut budget deficits to required levels.
Evening television newscasts gave the vote top billing and commentaries all said President Jacques Chirac had failed spectacurlarly in his bid for a "new elan."

"The French left has made it. It is approaching a veritable landslide victory," ARD correspondent Heiko Engelkes reported from Paris. "President Chirac is the clear loser. He wanted to win a bit of room to manoeuvre, he wanted to get a new elan for his conservative majority. That has now failed."

"A day of change in France and certainly a day of change in Europe," ZDF television commented. "The left has won a fat majority. The French don't dance to their president's tune. French President Chirac is sitting in the Elysee Palace this evening slapping himself in the face."

One of the first press editorials, from Monday's edition of the Neue Westfaelische newspaper, said the result was a protest against Chirac and "his broken campaign promises of a blossoming France and many hundred thousand new jobs."
The Bielefeld daily said Jospin had not made his own programme clear: "His left-wing alliance is somehow in favour of returning to a Europe of nations. The course is somehow unclear."

Germans have watched developments in the French campaign closely, especially since a dispute between Bonn and the powerful Bundesbank central bank has raised the possibility of Germany causing a delay in launching the euro.

The prospect of a new French government less committed to tough cuts in social spending to meet the tough Maastricht criteria for EMU has opened a range of new possibilities in hitherto strictly pro-European Bonn.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-left government has itself brought the Maastricht criteria into question by suddenly asking the Bundesbank to revalue its vast gold and currency reserves to provide more funds to help to qualify for EMU.
